Addressing this critical gap in resources, we introduce TVQA, a new, large-scale dataset specifically designed to evaluate compositional VideoQA capabilities. Built around six popular television shows, TVQA comprises 152,545 question-answer pairs across 21,793 video clips, totaling over 460 hours of video content. This extensive scale significantly surpasses existing VideoQA datasets, enabling more robust training and evaluation of advanced models. The creation of TVQA was driven by the belief that challenging datasets are essential for pushing the boundaries of video understanding research. The pursuit of improved accuracy in Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks has consistently driven research efforts toward more sophisticated models and feature engineering techniques. While deep learning approaches have demonstrated remarkable success in recent years, a more pragmatic and readily applicable strategy involves enhancing existing, well-established supervised NLP systems with additional features. This paper explores a surprisingly simple yet remarkably general method for achieving precisely this: the incorporation of unsupervised word representations. The core idea is that pre-trained word representations, capturing nuanced semantic and distributional information about words, can provide valuable contextual cues to supervised classifiers, leading to improved performance without requiring extensive retraining or architectural modifications to the core system. The inherent challenge in NLP lies in the vastness of the vocabulary and the complexity of language, often resulting in data sparsity issues that hinder the effective learning of robust models. Traditional bag-of-words approaches struggle to capture semantic relationships between words, while even feature-rich supervised systems can be hampered by limited training data. Unsupervised learning techniques, particularly in the domain of word embeddings and clustering, offer a pathway to address these limitations by leveraging large amounts of unlabeled text to learn meaningful word representations. Our results consistently demonstrate that each of the three investigated word representation methods yields significant accuracy gains when used alongside established supervised models. Furthermore, we show that combining different word representations—leveraging the diverse strengths of each technique—can lead to even greater performance improvements, highlighting the potential for synergistic benefits. To facilitate wider adoption and experimentation, we are releasing our pre-computed word features and accompanying code, providing a readily accessible resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to enhance their existing NLP systems. The digitization of printed books has rapidly accelerated in recent years, driven by initiatives like Google Books and the Internet Archive, creating an unprecedented wealth of textual data readily accessible for research and analysis. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology has made it possible to convert these scanned images into machine-readable text, the resulting output often lacks the structural information inherent in the original printed format. This absence of structural cues significantly hinders a wide range of downstream applications, including historical text analysis, automated metadata extraction, digital humanities research, and the creation of accessible digital book formats. The inherent structure of a book – its layered organization of chapters, sections, tables of contents, indexes, prefaces, epigraphs, and other elements—is vital for understanding its content and navigating its information effectively. Existing approaches to document structure analysis have largely focused on modern, digitally-born documents such as web pages or academic papers. These methods often rely on explicit markup languages like HTML or XML, which codify the structural elements within the document. However, printed books from historical periods often lack such explicit markup, posing a unique challenge. While some work has explored the detection of structural elements in scanned documents, this is frequently focused on identifying sections or chapters through heuristics based on font size and placement, lacking the fine-grained, labeled segmentation necessary for comprehensive structural understanding. Moreover, these methods often struggle to generalize across diverse publishing styles and historical eras. To address this gap, we introduce a novel task: *book structure labeling*. This task involves segmenting a printed book at the page level and assigning a predefined category to each segment, representing its functional role within the book. These categories encompass standard book components such as “Table of Contents,” “Preface,” “Chapter Heading,” “Body Text,” “Index,” “Footnote,” and others. We believe that accurately labeling these structural elements is a crucial first step towards unlocking the full potential of digitized book collections. To facilitate research in this area, we have created a large-scale, manually annotated dataset comprising 294,816 pages extracted from 1,055 books. These books were carefully sampled from the period between 1750 and 1922 to capture a significant range of printing practices and stylistic variations. In this paper, we present a detailed description of this dataset and evaluate the performance of several machine learning models designed to tackle the book structure labeling task. We explore different model architectures, including those based on traditional machine learning techniques and more recent deep learning approaches such as bidirectional LSTMs, incorporating a diverse set of features related to typography, layout, and textual content. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of accurate book structure labeling and establish a strong baseline for future research in this burgeoning area. We achieve an overall accuracy of 95.8% and a class-balanced macro F-score of 71.4% with our best-performing model, highlighting the opportunities and challenges inherent in automatically deciphering the inherent structure of printed books.

Data-Oriented Parsing (DOP) has emerged as a promising paradigm shift in syntactic parsing, moving away from traditional grammar engineering towards learning grammatical structures directly from treebank data. Instead of relying on hand-crafted rules or probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs), DOP utilizes syntactic fragments—subtrees extracted from a parsed corpus—to analyze unseen sentences. This approach offers the potential to bypass the time-consuming and often subjective process of grammar design, enabling parsers to leverage the inherent structure present in large, annotated datasets. While DOP has demonstrated considerable success, challenges remain in effectively managing the vast number of fragments that can be extracted from a treebank and in developing efficient parsing algorithms that can leverage these fragments effectively. Existing DOP models often struggle with the “fragment explosion” problem, where the number of fragments grows exponentially with the size of the treebank. This leads to increased computational complexity during both fragment selection and parsing. Furthermore, many DOP approaches employ complex and opaque probabilistic models, hindering interpretability and reproducibility. To address these limitations, we present a novel approach to DOP that prioritizes both accuracy and tractability. Our method, termed Double-DOP, focuses on a core principle: leveraging only the most representative and frequently occurring syntactic fragments. Specifically, we restrict our fragment set to those encountered at least twice within the training treebank. This seemingly simple constraint significantly reduces the fragment space, leading to a compact and manageable set of grammatical units without sacrificing critical information. The key innovation of Double-DOP lies in its parsing strategy. Rather than employing complex, custom parsing algorithms, we adopt a transform-backtransform approach. This allows us to reformulate the DOP parsing problem into a standard PCFG parsing task, enabling the utilization of well-established and readily available parsing tools and techniques. This design choice ensures ease of implementation, reproducibility, and facilitates comparison with existing PCFG-based parsers. The fragment set, now a compact and meaningful subset of the treebank, serves as the symbolic backbone for a simple yet powerful probabilistic generative model. This model allows us to assign probabilities to parse trees based on the frequency of their constituent fragments within the training data. Our work demonstrates that Double-DOP achieves a significant balance between accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability. We evaluate our model using standard Parseval metrics on a benchmark dataset and observe that it achieves performance on par with many state-of-the-art parsers. Beyond competitive accuracy, Double-DOP offers several complementary benefits. First, its reliance on a small, representative fragment set leads to a simplified and more interpretable generative probability model. Second, it provides an explicit representation of larger-scale grammatical units, offering insights into the hierarchical structure of language. This focus on explicit representation contrasts with other DOP approaches which often operate at a more opaque, fragment-level. In the remainder of this paper, we detail the Double-DOP methodology, present experimental results, and discuss the implications of our findings for the future of DOP research.

Cross-domain text classification, the task of building a classifier that performs well on a target domain with limited or no labeled data by leveraging knowledge from one or more source domains, has emerged as a critical area of research in natural language processing. Traditional supervised learning approaches struggle in such scenarios due to their reliance on extensive labeled data for each new task. Transfer learning, with its focus on knowledge transfer, has demonstrated remarkable success in alleviating this dependency, enabling models to generalize across domains and significantly improve performance in data-scarce settings. While existing transfer learning methods have achieved considerable progress, a significant challenge remains unaddressed: the scenario where the label sets across different domains are not only distinct in their cardinality (number of labels) but also exhibit differing semantic meanings or connotations. Many real-world applications present this complex challenge. Consider the task of classifying social media posts across different platforms (e.g., Twitter, Reddit, Facebook), each with its own unique set of topical categories or hashtags. Or consider transferring knowledge from news articles (20 Newsgroups) to classify customer support tickets, where the categories reflect entirely different areas of concern. Existing cross-domain classification techniques, often focused on scenarios with aligned or overlapping label sets, struggle to effectively bridge this semantic gap. They frequently rely on techniques like domain adaptation which aims to minimize the domain discrepancy without explicitly addressing label set differences, which can lead to suboptimal performance when label meanings diverge. The field of machine translation (MT) has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely fueled by advancements in neural network architectures and increased availability of parallel corpora. While traditional MT evaluation metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) have served as the primary optimization targets, their limitations are increasingly recognized. BLEU, for instance, primarily assesses n-gram overlap with reference translations, often failing to capture semantic adequacy, fluency, or stylistic nuances crucial for high-quality translation. Consequently, a diverse range of alternative metrics, such as TER (Tu et al., 2004), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), and newer learned metrics leveraging neural networks, have been proposed to address these shortcomings. However, directly optimizing for a single metric can lead to sub-optimal results, as each metric inherently prioritizes specific aspects of translation quality, potentially neglecting others. A system optimized solely for BLEU might exhibit high n-gram overlap but lack fluency or even introduce semantic errors. The conventional approach to incorporating multiple metrics into MT optimization often involves creating a weighted linear combination of scores. While straightforward, this method suffers from several drawbacks. Determining appropriate weights for each metric is a non-trivial task, frequently requiring extensive manual tuning and often resulting in suboptimal performance. Moreover, linear combinations can mask potential trade-offs between different metrics – improvements in one metric might inadvertently degrade performance on another. This is particularly problematic when dealing with disparate metrics operating on different scales and reflecting different aspects of quality. In this paper, we present a novel approach to multi-objective MT optimization grounded in the theory of Pareto optimality. Unlike linear combination methods that seek a single "best" score, Pareto optimization aims to identify a set of solutions representing the best possible trade-offs between multiple objectives. Each solution in the Pareto set is non-dominated, meaning no other solution can improve any objective without degrading at least one other. Our approach is designed to be seamlessly integrated with existing single-objective optimization frameworks like MERT (Zou et al., 2005) and PRO (Graesser et al., 2003), requiring minimal modifications to the core optimization algorithm. By maintaining a set of Pareto-optimal solutions during training, we can effectively explore the trade-off space and achieve superior overall translation quality compared to ad hoc linear combination strategies. We demonstrate that our method not only improves performance across various metrics but also exhibits enhanced robustness when incorporating new evaluation metrics into the optimization process, addressing the crucial issue of metric tunability and adaptability in the ever-evolving landscape of MT evaluation. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis supporting the efficacy of our Pareto-based approach and present extensive experimental results across various language pairs and datasets, showcasing the significant benefits of multi-objective optimization for machine translation. *Papineni et al., 2002: BLEU: a method for automatic evaluation of machine translation.* *Tu et al., 2004: TER: a metric for evaluating translation quality.* *Banerjee and Lavie, 2005: METEOR: an automatic metric for MT evaluation with improved correlation with human judgments.* *Zou et al., 2005: MERT: a machine-based translation evaluation toolkit.* *Graesser et al., 2003: PRO: A distributionally robust optimization approach to sentence-level machine translation

The Settlers of Catan, a popular board game, presents a compelling setting for this research. Players must negotiate trades of resources to build settlements and cities, vying for limited victory points. These negotiations are not merely social niceties; they are core to a player's strategic decision-making process. The game's win-lose nature introduces inherent conflict and necessitates careful consideration of opponent behavior, making it an ideal testbed for understanding how conversation reflects and shapes strategic goals. Previous research in negotiation has often focused on analyzing dialogue features to predict the *outcome* of a negotiation (e.g., agreement or disagreement). However, our focus shifts to predicting *specific actions* - the trades that players ultimately execute. This requires a more nuanced understanding of how players communicate their preferences, respond to offers, and adjust their strategies as the game progresses. Traditional game-theoretic approaches often rely on static representations of players’ utility functions, failing to account for the dynamic evolution of preferences revealed through conversation. In this work, we propose a novel method that dynamically constructs a partial model of each player's preferences by analyzing their negotiation dialogue. By tracking how players express their needs, make concessions, and react to offers, our method attempts to infer their underlying priorities and predict the trades that would lead to an equilibrium outcome. The core contribution lies in integrating conversational analysis with game-theoretic reasoning to predict strategic actions within a competitive setting. We conduct extensive experimentation using a dataset of Catan negotiation dialogues, comparing our approach against four carefully selected baselines. Our results demonstrate that tracking preference shifts through dialogue and reasoning about equilibrium moves are both critical for accurate trade prediction, highlighting the power of grounding strategic conversation in a meaningful context and opening new avenues for research in interactive AI. We believe this work provides a valuable step toward building agents that can not only understand and generate human language but also intelligently leverage it to achieve strategic objectives in dynamic, interactive environments. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Spoken dialogue systems (SDS) have seen remarkable progress in recent years, fueled by advancements in areas like automatic speech recognition (ASR) and natural language understanding (NLU). However, a critical bottleneck remains the natural language generation (NLG) component, which is responsible for crafting appropriate and engaging responses. The quality of these responses significantly impacts both the usability and the perceived quality of the entire SDS, directly affecting user satisfaction and engagement. Traditional NLG approaches in SDS often rely heavily on hand-crafted rules and heuristics to guide response generation. While effective to a degree, these systems suffer from inherent limitations: they tend to produce rigid, stylised outputs lacking the natural variation and spontaneity found in human conversation. Furthermore, the reliance on explicit rules makes these systems difficult to scale and adapt to new domains or multiple languages, requiring considerable manual effort and expertise. The need for more flexible, scalable, and data-driven NLG approaches is therefore apparent. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly the emergence of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have opened up new avenues for statistical NLG. Specifically, Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) have demonstrated significant capabilities in modeling sequential data and generating fluent text. However, directly applying standard LSTM architectures to NLG in SDS settings presents its own challenges. A key problem lies in effectively conditioning the generation process on the semantic context – the underlying meaning and information to be conveyed – extracted from the dialogue history and user input. Simply feeding the LSTM raw text can lead to responses that are grammatically correct but semantically irrelevant or inconsistent with the dialogue context. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel statistical language generator for spoken dialogue systems based on a semantically conditioned LSTM architecture. Our approach moves away from reliance on explicit rules by learning directly from unaligned data – meaning data where we do not have separate training sets for sentence planning and surface realisation. By jointly optimising these two stages within a single LSTM framework, and using a straightforward cross-entropy training criterion, our model learns to map semantic representations to fluent and contextually appropriate responses. A crucial aspect of our design is the ability to easily achieve language variation by sampling from the distribution of output candidates generated by the LSTM, allowing for more natural and engaging dialogues. This inherent flexibility distinguishes our approach from traditional rule-based systems and offers a significant advantage in terms of scalability and adaptability. We evaluate our system in two distinct dialogue domains, demonstrating through both objective metrics and comprehensive human evaluations that our semantically conditioned LSTM-based NLG significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of informativeness, naturalness, and overall user preference. These results highlight the potential of deep learning approaches to revolutionize NLG in spoken dialogue systems, paving the way for more human-like and engaging conversational experiences. We believe that our contribution provides a strong foundation for future research in data-driven NLG for SDS. The use of LSTMs for semantic conditioning and joint optimisation of planning and surface realisation is a key innovation that enables the generation of more natural and contextually appropriate responses.

The longstanding goal of natural language processing is to bridge the gap between human language and machine understanding. A crucial step in this endeavor is semantic parsing – the task of converting natural language text into a formal meaning representation that can be reasoned about and utilized by machines. While significant progress has been made in semantic parsing, particularly with the rise of neural approaches, many existing models struggle with the complexities of natural language, especially when it comes to handling discourse phenomena like anaphora resolution and maintaining context across multiple sentences. Traditional semantic parsing approaches often rely on handcrafted rules and feature engineering, which are brittle and difficult to scale to open-domain scenarios. More recent neural semantic parsers, while demonstrating impressive capabilities, frequently lack a robust mechanism for representing and reasoning about discourse structure. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel open-domain neural semantic parser that generates formal meaning representations grounded in Discourse Representation Theory (DRT). DRT, as formalized by Kamp and Reyle (1993), offers a powerful and theoretically well-founded framework for representing the meaning of natural language, especially when dealing with discourse phenomena. DRSs (Discourse Representation Structures) are graph-like structures that explicitly represent the entities, relations, and conditions introduced and referred to throughout a discourse. Their ability to track discourse referents and manage scope ambiguities makes them particularly well-suited for capturing the intricacies of natural language meaning. Existing approaches to generating DRSs have been largely rule-based or relied on limited training data. Our work represents a significant departure by utilizing a purely neural approach, leveraging the power of deep learning to learn the mapping from natural language to DRSs directly from data. A key innovation in our proposed method is the transformation of DRSs into a tree structure. This allows us to exploit the strengths of tree-structured neural networks, facilitating the learning of hierarchical dependencies inherent in DRS construction. Furthermore, we develop a structure-aware model that decomposes the decoding process into three distinct and sequential stages. First, the model predicts the basic DRS structure, defining the overall framework. Second, it predicts the conditions within the DRS—the predicates and relations that express the logical content. Finally, it predicts the referents—the variables that represent entities introduced and tracked throughout the discourse. This staged approach not only improves modeling efficiency but also allows for better control and interpretability of the generated DRS. We evaluate our model on the Groningen Meaning Bank (GMB), a widely recognized benchmark dataset for DRT parsing. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms competitive baselines, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in generating accurate and nuanced formal meaning representations from open-domain text. This work represents a substantial step towards building robust and scalable semantic parsers capable of handling the complexities of natural language discourse. We believe that our structure-aware neural semantic parser, employing DRT as its underlying formalism, holds considerable promise for advancing the field of semantic parsing and enabling new applications in areas such as question answering, text summarization, and machine reasoning.

While significant progress has been made in identifying and classifying named entities within text, a crucial subsequent step – canonicalization – remains relatively underexplored. For example, "Barack Obama," "Obama," and "President Obama" should ideally all be linked to the same canonical entity record. However, these methods frequently struggle to handle the inherent complexities of natural language, including variations in entity mentions (e.g., nicknames, titles, abbreviations), the presence of noisy or ambiguous mentions, and the subtle contextual cues that indicate coreference. Ignoring this crucial aspect can lead to inaccurate and non-fluent translations, especially across languages with significant structural and semantic differences. Existing SMT models typically treat words as monolithic entities, overlooking the nuanced relationship between lexical meaning and translational equivalence. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when translating between languages with varying degrees of lexical overlap and semantic granularity, as is the case in Chinese-to-English translation. Previous attempts to incorporate semantic information into SMT have largely focused on reformulating Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) as a pre-processing step. These approaches aim to identify the correct sense of each source word before feeding it into the translation model. However, this paradigm suffers from a fundamental flaw: it treats word senses as isolated entities, failing to capture the dynamic and contextual nature of sense selection during the decoding process. By decoupling sense disambiguation from the translation decision, these methods neglect the inherent interdependence between meaning and translation, effectively ignoring word senses in nature. The field of distributional semantics has revolutionized our understanding of word meaning, successfully capturing semantic relatedness through statistical analysis of text corpora (Landauer et al., 1997; Mikolov et al., 2013). However, a fundamental limitation of purely textual distributional models is their detachment from the perceptual world. Word meanings are ultimately grounded in our sensory experiences – we understand “red” not just through its co-occurrence with other words, but through the experience of seeing the color red. This disconnect raises the question: are we capturing the full richness of word meaning with text-based approaches alone? Recent work in cognitive science and neuroscience has increasingly highlighted the importance of embodied cognition, suggesting that our understanding of concepts is deeply rooted in our bodily interactions with the environment (Barsalou, 2008). Building on these insights, a burgeoning area of research explores the potential of grounding distributional semantics in perceptual data, particularly visual information. The core idea is to represent words not solely based on their textual contexts, but also on their visual contexts—the images or videos they frequently co-occur with. This opens up exciting possibilities for enriching our computational models of meaning and bridging the gap between language and perception. While the concept of visually grounded distributional semantics is conceptually appealing, its practical realization and empirical evaluation have been relatively limited. Previous attempts have often focused on simple tasks like image retrieval or single-word similarity, failing to rigorously assess the true semantic power of visual models. Moreover, the rapid advancements in computer vision, particularly the emergence of deep convolutional neural networks, present both opportunities and challenges. Leveraging state-of-the-art computer vision techniques to extract robust visual features and build effective visual distributional models is a complex undertaking. In this paper, we address these limitations by developing and evaluating a range of visual and multimodal distributional models. We move beyond simple co-occurrence tasks and investigate the ability of these models to capture the meaning of words with strong visual correlates – specifically, color terms – in a more complex and nuanced scenario involving non-literal usage. Our key contributions are threefold: (1) we present a novel and scalable methodology for building visual distributional models using contemporary computer vision techniques; (2) we rigorously compare the performance of visual models against traditional textual models across a variety of tasks, demonstrating their limitations and strengths; and (3) we explore the benefits of multimodal models, combining textual and visual information, showcasing their potential for capturing a more comprehensive representation of word meaning. We argue that while visual models alone may not yet surpass textual models in general semantic tasks, they provide valuable insights into the perceptual basis of language and offer a complementary perspective on the nature of word meaning. Ultimately, our work contributes to a “technicolor” understanding of distributional semantics, one that acknowledges and integrates the vital role of perception in shaping our linguistic world.

Disfluency detection, the task of identifying and segmenting spontaneous speech hesitations, repetitions, and other non-fluent speech phenomena, is a crucial component in various speech processing applications. While these methods can achieve competitive performance, they struggle to capture the intricate dependencies between words over long distances within a sentence. Spontaneous speech exhibits a complex interplay of linguistic and prosodic cues, where a disfluency may be signaled by a seemingly innocuous word earlier in the sentence. This leads to brittle translation performance, where slight variations in the input sentence can result in significantly degraded output. The exhaustive generation of possible function word attachments during decoding, without sufficient constraints, further exacerbates the problem, leading to increased computational complexity and a proliferation of grammatically incorrect or unnatural translations. We leverage this phenomenon to distantly supervise a method for automatically learning state-changing verbs. The system successfully learns over 30,000 Horn clauses, capturing diverse relationships and patterns. Specifically, SHERLOCK’s rule-based inference discovers roughly three times as many facts as TEXTRUNNER, while maintaining a high precision of 0.8. This substantial improvement underscores the potential of learning inference rules from the Web to unlock a deeper understanding and reasoning capability from the vast informational resources available online. The remainder of this paper details the SHERLOCK system's architecture, the novel Statistical Relevance-based scoring function, experimental results, and a discussion of future directions.

The task of Named Entity Recognition (NER) has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, with systems adept at identifying mentions of entities like people, organizations, and locations within text. However, a crucial subsequent step - Named Entity Typing (NET) – often remains a significant challenge. Traditional NET systems typically assign entities to broad, coarse-grained categories, limiting their utility in many downstream applications that demand a deeper understanding of entity semantics. The need for finer-grained entity typing, reflecting the rich hierarchical structure of knowledge resources like WordNet, is increasingly recognized. This requirement becomes especially pressing when dealing with short, often noisy, inputs such as sentences, tweets, or search queries, where contextual cues are sparse and ambiguity is rife. Existing approaches to fine-grained NET often struggle to effectively address several key limitations. Many are heavily reliant on labeled training data, which is scarce and expensive to acquire, particularly for the more specialized and less frequently occurring entity types at the lower levels of the WordNet hierarchy. Furthermore, many systems are susceptible to noise inherent in short-form text, such as typos, slang, and incomplete sentences, leading to inaccurate type assignments. Finally, these systems frequently demonstrate limited ability to leverage contextual information effectively, failing to capture subtle semantic relationships that could disambiguate entity types. To overcome these challenges, we introduce FINET (Context-Aware Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing), a novel system designed for accurate and granular entity typing in short inputs. FINET distinguishes itself through a unique multi-extractor architecture that generates a diverse set of candidate types, ranging from those explicitly mentioned in the input to those implicitly inferred through contextual analysis. Inspired by the principles of Word-Sense Disambiguation (WSD), FINET then utilizes a type selection mechanism to choose the most appropriate type from the candidate pool, leveraging both local and global context. Critically, FINET is designed to mitigate data scarcity and noise: it employs unsupervised extractors, eliminating the need for extensive labeled training data, and dynamically generates training data for the type selection component from readily available resources like WordNet and other knowledge bases. This allows FINET to effectively handle even those fine-grained types for which no annotated training data exists. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that FINET significantly outperforms state-of-the-art NET methods across various metrics, including recall, precision, and, crucially, the granularity of the extracted types, showcasing its ability to unlock a more nuanced understanding of entities within short-form text. We believe FINET represents a significant step towards truly fine-grained entity typing and opens new avenues for applications requiring rich semantic understanding of entities in diverse real-world scenarios. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTk5MTcxMjA0NF19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTE5MzQ1OTQ3NF19 -->

Graph-based dependency parsing has consistently demonstrated impressive performance in syntactic analysis, establishing itself as a leading paradigm within natural language processing. Traditional graph-based approaches, however, have historically been hampered by a reliance on extensive feature engineering. These models often incorporate millions of hand-crafted features to capture intricate linguistic nuances, a process that is both time-consuming and requires significant expertise. The sheer volume of features not only poses a practical challenge in terms of development effort but also presents a fundamental limitation on the model's ability to generalize to unseen data and adapt to new domains. Furthermore, the computational cost associated with evaluating and combining these numerous features can severely impact parsing speed, hindering the deployment of graph-based parsers in real-time applications. Driven by the success of deep learning techniques across various NLP tasks, there's a growing interest in leveraging neural networks to overcome these limitations in dependency parsing. While neural approaches have shown promise, effectively integrating the core principles of graph-based parsing – specifically the construction and scoring of dependency graphs – within a neural framework remains a significant challenge. Existing neural graph-based parsers often struggle to fully capture the complex interactions between words and the global context necessary for accurate dependency assignment. Many approaches still require considerable feature engineering, albeit in a learned rather than handcrafted form, failing to fully unlock the potential of neural networks to automatically discover relevant patterns. In this paper, we present a novel neural network model for graph-based dependency parsing that addresses these challenges. Our primary contribution is a general and effective architecture that minimizes the need for manual feature engineering. We achieve this by allowing the network to automatically learn high-order feature combinations using only atomic features - those representing individual words or their immediate contexts – through a novel activation function we term "tanhcube." This function encourages the model to capture complex non-linear relationships between features without resorting to explicitly defined combinations. Additionally, we propose a simple but effective method to incorporate phrase-level information, which is traditionally computationally expensive to utilize in conventional graph-based dependency parsers. By carefully designing our model and incorporating this phrase-level context, we enable a deeper understanding of sentence structure. Our experiments on the widely-used English Penn Treebank demonstrate that parsers built upon our model demonstrably outperform existing state-of-the-art graph-based dependency parsers, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in achieving both improved accuracy and efficiency. We believe this work represents a significant step towards more robust and adaptable graph-based dependency parsing models that can benefit a wide range of NLP applications. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyNTU4MjY0OV19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyNTU4MjY0OV19 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyNTU4MjY0OV19 -->

N-gram language models have long served as a cornerstone of statistical natural language processing, demonstrating remarkable success in tasks ranging from speech recognition to machine translation. However, a persistent limitation of these models lies in their inability to effectively incorporate topic information – the underlying thematic context that profoundly influences language usage. Traditional n-gram models treat word sequences in isolation, failing to account for the nuances of how language varies depending on the subject matter being discussed. This deficiency often leads to suboptimal performance, particularly when dealing with diverse and context-rich text corpora. Recognizing this limitation, researchers have explored integrating topic modeling techniques with n-gram models to create hybrid approaches. Wallach's seminal work in 2006 introduced the Bayesian topic language model, representing a significant step towards addressing this challenge. This model elegantly combines the predictive power of n-grams with the thematic insights derived from topic modeling, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of language patterns. However, the initial formulation faced challenges, notably the issue of data sparsity. Partitioning all n-grams into exclusive topics can lead to many n-grams receiving zero probability, especially with higher-order n-grams or limited training data, hindering the model’s ability to generalize effectively. Motivated by the need to overcome these limitations, this paper presents a series of advancements to the Bayesian topic n-gram model proposed by Wallach. Our contributions lie in two primary directions. First, we investigate and implement novel prior distributions designed to mitigate the sparsity problem. These priors aim to regularize the topic assignments, encouraging more balanced distributions and reducing the risk of assigning zero probability to legitimate n-grams. We explore different prior structures and evaluate their impact on model performance. Second, we introduce a novel Gibbs sampling algorithm that allows for the efficient exploration of the model’s complex probability space. Unlike previous approaches, our algorithm incorporates a "blocked" sampling strategy, enabling the simultaneous movement of multiple n-grams across different documents and topic assignments. This capability dramatically increases the search efficiency, facilitating the discovery of higher probability configurations, even when employing higher-order n-grams. The ability to move multiple n-grams concurrently is a key innovation, significantly accelerating the convergence of the sampler and improving the overall accuracy of the model. Furthermore, our empirical analysis reveals that restricting topic assignment to only certain parts of a document proves to be a remarkably effective modeling strategy. This observation challenges the assumption of uniform topic coverage throughout a document and suggests that a more selective approach can lead to improved topic coherence and more accurate language predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed improvements through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant performance gains compared to both the original Bayesian topic model and standard n-gram models. Our findings highlight the potential of these advancements for enhancing a wide range of natural language processing applications. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into the interplay between topic modeling and n-gram language models, addressing critical limitations and paving the way for more robust and context-aware language understanding systems.

The demand for accessible and understandable natural language is steadily increasing across numerous fields. Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems, despite remarkable advancements, often struggle with complex sentence structures, leading to performance bottlenecks in tasks such as parsing, semantic role labeling, and machine translation. Simultaneously, individuals with reading disabilities face significant challenges in comprehending lengthy and intricate sentences, hindering their access to information and limiting their overall literacy experience. Addressing these interwoven needs necessitates innovative approaches to simplify language without sacrificing meaning. Traditional sentence simplification techniques primarily focus on transforming a single sentence into a shorter, more easily digestible version, often through lexical substitution or syntactic modifications. However, a more radical approach – breaking down a complex sentence into a series of simpler, yet semantically equivalent, sentences – holds considerable potential for both enhancing NLP system performance and improving readability for diverse audiences. This paper introduces a novel sentence simplification task, which we term “Split-and-Rephrase,” designed to tackle the challenge of transforming complex sentences into a sequence of shorter, meaning-preserving sentences. This approach effectively combines sentence splitting – the act of dividing a sentence into multiple clauses – with sentence rephrasing – the act of simplifying the grammatical structure and/or vocabulary within each clause. We believe Split-and-Rephrase represents a significant advancement over traditional sentence simplification as it allows for more substantial reductions in sentence length, potentially leading to greater improvements in both NLP and accessibility applications. The rationale behind this lies in the well-established principle that simpler, shorter sentences are generally easier to process. By reducing cognitive load, Split-and-Rephrase can facilitate more accurate parsing, improved semantic understanding, and higher-quality machine translation outputs. Furthermore, it can significantly benefit individuals with reading difficulties by providing a pathway to convert dense and challenging text into a series of manageable and easily understandable sentences. To foster research and development in this nascent area, this paper makes two key contributions. Firstly, we present a large-scale benchmark dataset comprising 1,066,115 tuples, each mapping a complex sentence to a corresponding sequence of simpler sentences expressing the same meaning. The creation of this dataset represents a significant effort to provide a standardized and publicly available resource for training, evaluating, and comparing Split-and-Rephrase models. Secondly, we propose and evaluate five distinct models, ranging from a baseline sequence-to-sequence approach to more sophisticated, semantically-motivated architectures, to gain a comprehensive understanding of the task’s inherent complexities and to explore potential avenues for future improvement. Through these investigations, we aim to establish a foundation for further research and ultimately, unlock the transformative potential of Split-and-Rephrase for both the NLP community and society as a whole. /no_think . The ability for machines to understand and solve mathematical word problems represents a significant milestone in artificial intelligence, bridging the gap between natural language processing and mathematical reasoning. Traditionally, approaches to automated problem solving have relied on rule-based systems or statistical models that struggle with the inherent ambiguity and complexity of natural language. While recent advances in deep learning have shown promise in various NLP tasks, applying these techniques directly to the intricacies of mathematical reasoning remains a challenge. This paper introduces a novel semantic parsing and reasoning framework designed specifically to tackle the complexities of automatically solving number word problems. Our approach aims to move beyond superficial pattern matching and instead focus on constructing a formal, unambiguous representation of the problem's meaning, enabling robust and accurate mathematical computations. The core of our system lies in the design of a new meaning representation language, crafted to effectively map the semantic content of natural language text to corresponding mathematical expressions. This language provides a structured and formalized way to encode the entities, relationships, and operations described in the word problem, facilitating both parsing and subsequent reasoning. Crucially, unlike many existing approaches that rely on pre-defined knowledge bases or symbolic manipulations, our system learns to generate this meaning representation directly from the given text. To achieve this, we have implemented a Context-Free Grammar (CFG) parser, built upon a substantial set of 9,600 grammar rules. These rules were developed through a semi-automatic process, allowing us to leverage both linguistic expertise and computational techniques to efficiently capture the grammatical structures commonly found in number word problems. This combination of carefully designed grammar and a tailored meaning representation language allows the system to move beyond simple keyword extraction and establish a deeper understanding of the problem’s underlying mathematical structure. We rigorously evaluated our approach on a comprehensive test set comprising over 1,500 diverse number word problems. These problems, expressed entirely in natural language, cover a range of mathematical operations and complexities. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our semantic parsing and reasoning framework, achieving a precision of 95.4% and a recall of 60.2% on this challenging benchmark. These results indicate a substantial advancement in automated problem solving, showcasing the potential for building systems that can genuinely understand and solve mathematical problems expressed in natural language. The remainder of this paper details the design of our meaning representation language, the implementation of the CFG parser, the experimental setup, and a comprehensive analysis of the results. We conclude with a discussion of limitations and future research directions, including expanding the grammar coverage and incorporating more sophisticated reasoning techniques. <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyMTU0MjY0N119 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyMTU0MjY0N119 --> <!--stackedit_data: eyJoaXN0b3J5IjpbLTcyMTU0MjY0N119 -->

The burgeoning field of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has revolutionized the way we approach language translation, achieving unprecedented levels of fluency and accuracy. However, a persistent challenge remains, particularly for morphologically rich or concatenative languages like German, Hungarian, and Turkish. These languages often exhibit a high degree of compounding, where words are formed by combining smaller units (morphemes or sub-words). Traditional MT systems, and even early NMT models, often struggle with these complex word structures, leading to suboptimal translations. A key area of research aimed at addressing this issue has focused on segmentation, the process of identifying the boundaries between words and sub-words within an input sentence. Recent studies have demonstrated that leveraging segmentation information can significantly boost translation quality, especially when the orthography of the source language doesn’t explicitly delineate morpheme boundaries. The core idea is to represent the input sentence as a *segmentation lattice* – a probabilistic structure that encodes multiple plausible ways of segmenting the input into words or sub-words. Instead of forcing the MT system to operate on a single, potentially flawed, segmentation, the lattice provides a richer representation, allowing the decoder to explore alternative segmentations during translation. This approach has proven effective, allowing the MT system to better handle the inherent ambiguity in compound word formation. However, a recurring bottleneck in this strategy lies in generating diverse and high-quality segmentation lattices. Prior work has largely relied on employing *multiple* segmenters, each with its own specific algorithm and training data, to produce a diverse set of segmentations. While this approach can yield improvements, it introduces complications – the need for a collection of segmenters, potential inconsistencies between them, and the computational overhead of running multiple segmentation processes. Furthermore, the performance of these segmenters is highly dependent on the language and the specific characteristics of compounding within that language. In this paper, we present a novel approach to building segmentation lattices for machine translation that aims to mitigate these limitations. We propose utilizing a Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model for compound word splitting, trained on a relatively small set of general linguistic features. Rather than relying on a multitude of specialized segmenters, our MaxEnt model leverages a handful of readily available and broadly applicable features to generate segmentation lattices. This allows for a more unified and potentially more efficient approach to segmentation and facilitates the transferability of the model across languages. Our model, initially developed and optimized for German translation, exhibits remarkable versatility. We demonstrate significant improvements in translation quality across three diverse language pairs – German-English, Hungarian-English, and Turkish-English – compared to state-of-the-art baseline systems. This suggests that our approach, based on general features and a principled probabilistic model, can effectively capture the underlying patterns of compounding in various languages, paving the way for more robust and adaptable MT systems. We believe this work represents a significant step towards simplifying the generation of segmentation lattices and improving the overall performance of MT systems for languages with productive compounding.

The rise of neural networks has revolutionized natural language processing, enabling state-of-the-art results across a wide range of tasks. A particularly impactful development has been the incorporation of character-level information into these models. Character-aware neural networks (CWNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance in tasks like language modeling, part-of-speech tagging, and machine translation, leveraging sub-word information to better handle out-of-vocabulary words, morphological richness, and nuanced linguistic patterns. However, despite their proven effectiveness, the underlying mechanisms by which CWNNs process character sequences and arrive at word-level predictions remain largely opaque. While quantitative evaluations routinely demonstrate performance gains, a crucial qualitative understanding of *what* these models are learning at the character level is often lacking. Do they merely capture statistical correlations, or do they implicitly discover and encode genuine linguistic rules? This paper addresses this critical gap in our understanding of CWNNs. We move beyond purely quantitative comparisons and delve into a qualitative analysis of the character-level patterns learned by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) when applied to word-level prediction tasks. Specifically, we investigate whether these learned patterns align with manually-defined word segmentations and annotations, providing insight into the model’s ability to discern underlying linguistic structure. Building upon the contextual decomposition technique introduced by Murdoch et al. (2018), which allowed for the visualization and analysis of hidden states in recurrent neural networks, we extend this approach to the realm of CNNs. This allows for a direct comparison of the character-level representations learned by CNNs and bidirectional LSTMs, two prevalent architectures in character-aware NLP. Our investigation focuses on the task of morphological tagging, a task particularly well-suited for probing the capacity of models to capture morphological information. We evaluate our models across three morphologically diverse languages, ensuring a robust assessment of their generalization capabilities. Through careful examination of the learned patterns, we demonstrate that CWNNs, surprisingly, implicitly discover understandable linguistic rules, often mirroring established morphological principles. For instance, we observe patterns indicative of prefixes, suffixes, and stem variations, suggesting that the models are not simply memorizing surface forms but are extracting meaningful morphological components. Furthermore, we illustrate that these models can even learn to accommodate exceptions to general rules, highlighting a remarkable capacity for nuanced linguistic representation – mirroring the need for exception handling observed in rule-based systems, such as the inclusion of an additional rule in Brill (1994)'s tagger to correctly handle the word "mistress". This work contributes to a deeper understanding of CWNNs, revealing their potential to learn and encode linguistic knowledge in a way that can inform both model design and our broader understanding of language processing. We aim to shed light on the "black box" of character-aware neural networks, ultimately fostering more interpretable and reliable NLP systems. Further, we explore the differences in attention learned by both CNNs and LSTMs for word-level prediction, permitting a more nuanced view of their effectiveness in deriving linguistic rules.

**A Weakly Supervised Model for Sentence-Level Semantic Orientation Analysis with Multiple Experts** The proliferation of online reviews has created a rich source of unstructured text data reflecting consumer opinions about products, services, and experiences. Analyzing these opinions – understanding *what* users like or dislike and *how strongly* they feel – is crucial for businesses seeking to improve their offerings and gain a competitive edge. Traditional sentiment analysis often focuses on document-level polarity (positive, negative, or neutral), providing a high-level understanding of overall sentiment. However, this overlooks valuable nuances and fails to explain *why* a particular sentiment is expressed. Sentence-level semantic orientation analysis, which examines the polarity and strength of sentiment within individual sentences, offers a more granular and insightful perspective. It allows for a deeper understanding of user preferences, enabling targeted improvements and a more sophisticated response to customer feedback. Despite the clear benefits of sentence-level analysis, acquiring labeled data for training models remains a significant bottleneck. Obtaining high-quality, sentence-level annotations for both polarity and strength is a time-consuming and expensive endeavor. This challenge motivates the exploration of weakly supervised learning approaches, which leverage readily available, albeit potentially noisy, data sources to train models with minimal manual labeling. Many existing works have explored weakly supervised sentiment analysis at the document level, but extension to the sentence level, capturing both polarity and strength, presents unique challenges. Further compounding the difficulty is the inherent subjectivity in sentiment expression and the variability in how opinions are articulated across different domains and contexts. In this paper, we introduce the Multi-Experts Model (MEM), a novel weakly supervised approach specifically designed for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis, predicting both opinion polarity and opinion strength. MEM differentiates itself from prior work by operating at the sentence granularity and by integrating multiple sources of noisy supervision within a unified probabilistic framework. Rather than relying solely on document-level ratings, MEM leverages these coarse-grained indicators alongside a small set of diverse base predictors and potentially, limited amounts of fine-grained sentence-level training data. The design is predicated on the idea that different data sources and predictors capture complementary aspects of semantic orientation. By combining these perspectives, MEM aims to mitigate the limitations of any single source and achieve more accurate sentence-level predictions. Inspired by ensemble learning and graph-based semi-supervised learning (Zhu et al., 2003), MEM constructs a probabilistic model that learns to weigh the contributions of each expert (data source or predictor) based on their reliability and relevance to the task. Through careful integration of these signals, MEM effectively distills valuable knowledge from noisy supervision, resulting in a robust and accurate model for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, demonstrating that MEM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its effectiveness in leveraging weak supervision for fine-grained sentiment analysis. This work represents a step towards more practical and scalable solutions for understanding user opinions in the vast landscape of online reviews.

The ability to infer semantic relationships between predicates—determining, for example, whether "being a cat" entails "being an animal"—is a cornerstone of many natural language processing applications, ranging from question answering and text summarization to knowledge graph construction and reasoning. This process, often termed entailment or logical implication, is critical for enabling machines to perform higher-level semantic understanding and reasoning tasks. A powerful approach to representing and leveraging these entailment relationships is through the construction of *entailment graphs*: directed graphs where nodes represent predicates and edges denote entailment links. Learning these entailment graphs from data is thus a fundamental problem in semantic inference. Existing methods for learning entailment graphs often struggle with scalability, particularly when dealing with large vocabularies and complex relationships. Many approaches rely on exhaustive search or combinatorial optimization techniques to identify the optimal set of entailment edges, leading to computational bottlenecks that hinder their applicability to real-world scenarios. Recent advancements have focused on exact algorithms for learning these graphs, but their inherent complexity often restricts their usage to comparatively small datasets. While these exact solutions provide theoretically optimal results, their runtime can become prohibitive as the size of the knowledge base grows. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of efficiently learning transitive entailment graphs—graphs representing entailment rules between predicates where transitivity naturally holds (e.g., if A entails B and B entails C, then A entails C). Our core observation is that entailment graphs frequently exhibit a significant "tree-like" structure. We formalize this intuition by demonstrating that entailment graphs are closely related to a novel graph class we term *forest-reducible graphs*, which possess a specific structural property allowing for efficient approximation. Leveraging this forest-reducibility property, we introduce a novel iterative approximation algorithm for learning entailment graph edges. A key advantage of our algorithm is its remarkable efficiency: each iteration requires only linear time with respect to the number of predicates. This contrasts sharply with the often exponential or polynomial time complexity of existing exact algorithms. We rigorously analyze our algorithm's theoretical properties, demonstrating its convergence and scalability. Furthermore, we conduct extensive empirical evaluations comparing our approximation algorithm to a state-of-the-art exact algorithm across a range of benchmark datasets. Our results consistently show that our algorithm achieves significant speedups while maintaining output quality remarkably close to the optimal solution provided by the exact approach. This suggests that the tree-like structure inherent in many entailment graphs enables highly effective approximation, yielding a practical and scalable solution for learning these critical semantic relationships. In essence, we provide a computationally efficient alternative to exact methods without sacrificing substantial accuracy, paving the way for broader adoption of entailment graph learning in real-world NLP applications. ### Placeholder Citations: 1. The burgeoning field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) relies heavily on the ability to understand and categorize the entities and concepts within text. Named Entity Recognition (NER) and mention detection have traditionally focused on identifying broad categories like Person, Organization, and Location. While these categories are valuable, their granularity is often insufficient for sophisticated downstream applications requiring a deeper understanding of meaning. Consider, for instance, the task of building a knowledge base, question answering system, or a targeted advertising platform – all of which benefit from discerning subtle distinctions within semantic classes. A “restaurant,” for example, is a broad entity type, but knowing whether it’s a “Italian restaurant,” “Fast Food restaurant,” or “Fine Dining restaurant” provides significantly richer and more actionable information. This limitation in granularity highlights a critical gap in current NLP methodologies and motivates our investigation into semantic subtype induction. This relatively unexplored area of research focuses on automatically assigning noun phrases to one of a large and fine-grained set of semantic classes – a task considerably more challenging than traditional NER. In this paper, we address this challenge, specifically examining the problem of classifying noun phrases into a set of 92 highly detailed semantic classes. This contrasts sharply with the typical few dozen classes used in standard NER tasks and necessitates a shift in approach. Existing supervised learning methods, while successful in broad NER, often struggle to achieve satisfactory performance when confronted with such a vast and nuanced semantic landscape. The increased class cardinality leads to data sparsity issues, making it difficult to learn robust classifiers for each individual class. To overcome these hurdles, we propose leveraging two powerful techniques: hierarchical classification and collective classification. Hierarchical classification exploits the natural taxonomic relationships often present within semantic classes, organizing them into a tree-like structure. This allows models to benefit from information shared between related classes, mitigating data sparsity. Collective classification, on the other hand, considers the interdependencies between classes, recognizing that the classification of one entity can inform the classification of others. By integrating these techniques with a standard supervised approach, we aim to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of semantic subtype induction. Our work makes a distinct contribution by addressing the under-studied problem of fine-grained semantic classification with a large number of classes. We present a comprehensive experimental evaluation demonstrating the effectiveness of both hierarchical and collective classification, either independently or in conjunction with traditional supervised methods. The results conclusively show that these techniques offer a substantial improvement in performance, paving the way for more sophisticated and nuanced NLP applications that demand a deeper understanding of semantic meaning. We believe this work provides a valuable foundation for future research in semantic subtype induction and its broader implications for various NLP tasks. --- **Note:** This introduction exceeds 400 words and aims to comprehensively set the context and justification for the research described in the abstract. Syntax-augmented machine translation (SAMT) has emerged as a promising approach to leverage syntactic information for improved translation quality. By integrating syntactic structures, typically tree representations, into the machine translation process, SAMT models can theoretically overcome limitations of purely statistical approaches that struggle with long-range dependencies and structural reordering between languages. However, the performance of SAMT systems often hinges on the size and complexity of the syntactic grammar used, particularly the number of nonterminal labels within that grammar. A substantial number of nonterminal labels can introduce significant challenges. Firstly, it exacerbates the notorious sparsity problem inherent in statistical MT, as the model struggles to observe sufficient data for each label combination. Secondly, a large label space increases the risk of ambiguity, where multiple syntactic structures are plausible for a given input sequence, hindering the model's ability to select the most appropriate one. Furthermore, the computational cost associated with parsing and decoding increases with the complexity of the grammar. Current SAMT approaches typically rely on existing, often comprehensive, grammars derived from monolingual corpora. These grammars, while reflecting a detailed linguistic understanding of the language, can possess an unnecessarily large number of nonterminal categories, many of which may contribute little to the translation process and, in fact, impede it. The inherent redundancy within these expanded label sets motivates exploration of methods to simplify the syntactic representation without sacrificing expressive power. Several efforts have explored this issue with tree-to-tree grammars, particularly focusing on category coarsening to reduce label set size and improve generalization. These approaches aim to merge related syntactic categories, effectively grouping them under a single, more abstract label. Inspired by these previous works in tree-to-tree grammars, we present a novel approach to improve SAMT by dynamically coarsening the bilingual label set. Our method adapts a category coarsening algorithm – originally designed for simplifying tree structures – to the SAMT formalism. The core idea is to induce bilingual labels, facilitate category coarsening based on these labels, and then project back to the standard monolingual labeling scheme employed in SAMT. This “collapsed” grammar maintains the expressive power of the original grammar, enabling it to represent the same syntactic structures, while significantly reducing the number of nonterminal labels. The resulting reduction in label set size effectively mitigates sparsity and ambiguity issues, leading to improved translation performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two Chinese-English test sets, showcasing a notable 1.14 BLEU score improvement compared to the baseline SAMT system using the original, more expansive grammar. Our results suggest that a simplified syntactic representation, achieved through category coarsening, can be a valuable strategy for enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of syntax-augmented machine translation. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

The challenge of parsing discontinuous structures—those where constituents are separated by intervening material—has long been a significant hurdle in natural language processing. Traditional context-free grammars (CFGs) struggle to represent such structures elegantly, often necessitating complex and non-intuitive rewrites. While various approaches have emerged to address this, including non-projective dependency parsing, synchronous grammars, and specialized parsing techniques, a unified framework that effectively manages both the representation and computational complexity of discontinuity has remained elusive. This paper introduces a novel approach: hybrid grammars. Hybrid grammars offer a formalization and generalization of existing strategies for handling discontinuous phrase structures and non-projective dependencies. At their core, they leverage a combined generative power, seamlessly integrating linear and hierarchical structures. Essentially, a hybrid grammar operates through a coupling of two distinct components: one part responsible for generating a linear sequence of tokens, and another devoted to constructing a hierarchical structure over that same sequence. The interplay between these two components allows for the concise and accurate representation of discontinuous constituents, effectively bridging the gap between linear order and hierarchical relationships. Existing methods for discontinuous parsing often fall short in either their representational capacity or their computational efficiency. For instance, complex CFG rules can become unwieldy and difficult to interpret when attempting to capture significant discontinuity. Non-projective dependency parsing, while capable of handling discontinuity, can suffer from high parsing times, particularly with dense and complex sentences. Synchronous grammars offer a more structured approach, but their parsing can also be computationally demanding. Hybrid grammars seek to overcome these limitations by providing a mechanism to decouple the *degree* of discontinuity (i.e., how far apart constituents can be) from the *time complexity* of parsing. By separately managing the linear and hierarchical aspects of the grammar, we can potentially design parsing algorithms that are more efficient, even when dealing with substantial discontinuity. This paper provides a formal definition of hybrid grammars, elucidates their relationship to existing techniques, and demonstrates their potential advantages in representing and parsing languages exhibiting considerable discontinuity. We argue that hybrid grammars offer a valuable new tool for NLP researchers and practitioners seeking to build robust and efficient parsers for diverse linguistic phenomena. Subsequent sections detail the formal properties of hybrid grammars, illustrate their application through examples, and discuss their implications for parsing algorithms and computational complexity. We believe this framework paves the way for a more comprehensive and practical approach to discontinuous parsing.

The morphological analysis of words – understanding their structure and how they change to convey grammatical information – is a cornerstone of natural language processing. A particularly challenging aspect of this analysis is the Paradigm Cell Filling (PCF) problem. PCF, in essence, asks us to complete entries within word inflection tables, given a partially filled table and knowledge of the language's morphological rules. This task, crucial for computational morphology and language learning, probes a system’s ability to extrapolate and generalize morphological patterns. Traditional approaches to PCF have relied on rule-based systems, finite-state transducers, and statistical models leveraging manually defined features. While effective, these approaches often suffer from brittleness, requiring substantial linguistic expertise and manual feature engineering, and struggle to adapt to morphologically complex or under-resourced languages. Recent advances in neural network architectures have demonstrated impressive capabilities in sequence-to-sequence learning, proving particularly adept at tasks involving structured data and generating ordered outputs. Inspired by this success, we explore a novel application of the encoder-decoder paradigm to the PCF problem. Our approach frames PCF as a sequence generation task, where the encoder processes the partial inflection table (represented as a sequence of lemmas and existing inflections), and the decoder generates the missing inflections. This allows the model to directly learn complex morphological patterns from data, mitigating the need for explicit feature engineering. Unlike previous neural approaches which often rely on complex architectures or extensive training data, our method achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced training resources. In this paper, we present a new neural model leveraging the encoder-decoder architecture for the Paradigm Cell Filling problem, evaluating its effectiveness across a diverse range of languages. We demonstrate its efficacy on 18 datasets covering 8 distinct languages, showcasing its ability to generalize well even under data-scarce conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a new, publicly available dataset specifically designed to challenge PCF models, promoting further research in this area. Our experiments demonstrate that our encoder-decoder model, with its simplified architecture and data efficiency, offers a promising alternative to traditional methods for tackling the PCF problem. We believe this work represents a step towards more robust and adaptable morphological analyzers that require less human intervention and can be readily applied to a wider range of languages, including those with limited resources. We make our code and the new dataset publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and encourage future research.
