Adapting existing models to support varying levels of granularity can be challenging, often requiring extensive retraining or complex architectural modifications. To address these challenges, we introduce Latent Predictor Networks (LPNs), a novel neural network architecture designed for modular and adaptable conditioning in language generation. LPNs move beyond the traditional paradigm of fixed conditioning contexts by incorporating a set of learnable "predictor" networks. Each predictor specializes in processing a specific aspect of the input, and the model learns to dynamically select and weight these predictors during generation. We extensively evaluate LPNs against strong baseline models on these newly created datasets, as well as a third established code generation corpus, demonstrating significant improvements in generation quality through the marginalization of multiple predictors. Our results highlight the promise of LPNs as a flexible and scalable architecture for conditional language generation, with particular relevance to code generation and other tasks requiring integration of structured and unstructured inputs. The task of multi-document summarization aims to condense multiple related documents into a shorter, coherent summary that captures the salient information. Traditional approaches to this problem often treat documents as independent entities, disregarding the underlying thematic coherence that frequently binds them together. However, in many real-world scenarios, documents are grouped by category—news articles about a specific event, scientific papers on a particular topic, or product reviews for a single item. This inherent categorization provides a rich source of information that can be leveraged to improve the quality of automatically generated summaries. This paper argues that explicitly incorporating category-specific information into the summarization process leads to significant improvements in content selection and overall summary quality. We hypothesize that sentences deemed important within a given category are likely to be more representative and informative than sentences selected solely based on their importance across the entire document collection. This insight leads us to introduce the concept of Category-Specific Importance (CSI), a metric designed to quantify the degree to which a sentence is characteristic of its document category. Unlike previous work that relies on external knowledge sources or specialized corpora, our approach makes use of readily available document content and syntactic structure to estimate CSI. We operationalize this through the introduction of two novel features, which can be efficiently computed without requiring pre-existing category labels. These features capture both the semantic relatedness of a sentence to its document set and its syntactic specificity to the category, enabling a nuanced assessment of a sentence's importance within a particular thematic context. Beyond demonstrating the utility of CSI in settings where document-to-category mappings are available, we further explore the generalization potential of our approach. Recognizing that manual annotation of document categories can be costly and time-consuming, we investigate the feasibility of automatic document categorization. We demonstrate that even in scenarios where category assignments are determined automatically, incorporating category-specific information into the summarization process still yields demonstrably better results. To facilitate practical application and reproducibility, we have integrated these CSI-based features into SWING (Summarization With INtegrated Category Guidance), a simple yet effective open-source extractive summarization system. SWING's architecture prioritizes clarity and efficiency, making it accessible to researchers and practitioners alike. Remarkably, in the competitive TAC-2011 guided summarization task, SWING consistently outperformed all other participating systems as evaluated by standard ROUGE metrics. This achievement underscores the efficacy of our category-specific approach and its potential to advance the state-of-the-art in multi-document summarization. The burgeoning field of natural language processing (NLP) has long benefited from advancements in computational hardware. While CPUs have traditionally served as the workhorses for NLP tasks, the increasing complexity of modern language models and parsing algorithms has spurred exploration into leveraging the parallel processing capabilities of GPUs. Graphics processing units, initially designed for rendering computer graphics, excel at performing the same operation on a massive dataset concurrently, a characteristic that aligns well with many machine learning techniques. However, a fundamental challenge arises when applying GPUs to NLP algorithms, which are often intrinsically designed to exploit *structural sparsity* – the fact that many potential computations are irrelevant due to the hierarchical nature of language. Traditional NLP algorithms meticulously prune the search space to avoid evaluating unnecessary derivations, a strategy that doesn't readily translate to the dense-operation paradigm of GPUs. Recent efforts have begun to bridge this gap. Canny et al. (2013) demonstrated a significant breakthrough by sacrificing the benefits of sparsity in favor of raw computational power, paving the way for GPU-accelerated Viterbi parsing. Their approach achieved impressive speeds, reaching approximately 164 sentences per second on a mid-range GPU while maintaining high parsing accuracy. This work highlighted the considerable potential of GPUs for parsing, albeit with a trade-off in efficiency. However, the inherent advantage of exploiting sparsity in NLP remains compelling, as it aligns with the cognitive processes underlying human language understanding and can lead to more interpretable and resource-efficient models. In this paper, we revisit the challenge of GPU parsing with a renewed focus on reintroducing sparsity without sacrificing speed. We adapt a coarse-to-fine pruning strategy—a technique commonly employed in CPU-based parsers to efficiently limit search space—to the constraints of a GPU architecture. By intelligently pruning unlikely parsing derivations during the parsing process, we significantly reduce the computational burden on the GPU, leading to substantial performance gains. Our approach achieves over 404 Viterbi parses per second on the same hardware used by Canny et al., representing a greater than 2x speedup. Beyond Viterbi parsing, we further extend our pruning technique to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) inference, a more sophisticated parsing algorithm known to produce more accurate results. Remarkably, we observe nearly a 6x speedup in MBR parsing throughput – increasing from 32 to over 190 sentences per second – when using our pruning technique. These results demonstrate that sparsity and GPU acceleration are not mutually exclusive and that a judicious combination of these approaches can lead to both faster and more accurate parsing systems. We believe our work represents a significant step towards unlocking the full potential of GPUs for a wide range of NLP tasks, where sparsity plays a crucial role. This work builds upon the foundations laid by Canny et al. (2013) and contributes a novel method for efficiently integrating sparsity into GPU parsing, addressing a key limitation of prior approaches and facilitating the development of more scalable and accurate NLP systems.

The task of spellchecking and autocorrection is a fundamental component of many natural language processing applications, from text editors to virtual assistants. Traditionally, robust spellcheckers relied heavily on manually annotated training data – large datasets of correctly spelled words, misspellings, and corresponding corrections – which is a resource-intensive and time-consuming process. This reliance on handcrafted resources presents a significant barrier to the deployment of effective spellcheckers in languages with limited annotation availability, a scenario encountered for the vast majority of the world’s languages. While dictionary-based approaches offer a baseline level of accuracy, they often struggle to handle novel misspellings or accurately predict the intended word in context, particularly when dealing with evolving language usage and user-specific errors. Recent advancements in language modeling and the sheer scale of data available on the World Wide Web have opened up the possibility of developing spellcheckers that operate without requiring substantial manual annotation. The web provides an unparalleled source of textual data, reflecting a broad spectrum of writing styles, vocabulary, and common errors. Leveraging this resource presents the opportunity to build language-independent spellchecking systems that can be rapidly adapted to new languages. However, the inherent noisiness of web data – containing typos, grammatical errors, and stylistic variations – poses a significant challenge. Previous attempts to utilize web data for language modeling have largely focused on refining data cleaning techniques or integrating dictionary-based corrections as a post-processing step. A more holistic approach, which directly incorporates the web’s inherent noisiness into the spellchecking and correction process, has been relatively unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a novel, end-to-end spellchecking and autocorrection system, termed “WebSpell,” that eschews the need for manually annotated training data by harnessing the World Wide Web as a massive, noisy corpus. Our system infers knowledge about common misspellings and word usage directly from web data to construct both an error model and an n-gram language model. Critically, we do not attempt to cleanse the web data but rather leverage its statistical properties to model the probability of different spelling variations. To further refine the system’s performance, we utilize a small secondary dataset—a set of news texts with artificially inserted misspellings—to tune confidence classifiers, allowing WebSpell to prioritize more reliable corrections. This approach enables the system to be readily instantiated for new languages, simply by collecting a large corpus of web text in the target language. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over dictionary-based baselines on human-typed data containing real misspellings in both English and German, achieving a total error rate of 3.8% in English. Furthermore, preliminary results on artificially generated data for Russian and Arabic suggest the scalability and potential of WebSpell across a diverse range of linguistic environments. This work represents a significant step towards truly language-independent spellchecking and autocorrection, overcoming the limitations of traditional approaches and paving the way for wider accessibility of these crucial language tools.

Question Answering over Knowledge Bases (KB-QA) has emerged as a pivotal area within Natural Language Processing (NLP), aiming to automatically generate answers to questions posed in natural language by leveraging the structured information stored within knowledge bases (KBs). The ultimate goal is to bridge the gap between human language and machine-understandable data, enabling more intuitive and efficient access to vast repositories of knowledge. While KB-QA has seen significant advancements, effectively addressing *simple* questions remains a surprisingly challenging task. Simple questions, frequently representing the majority of queries encountered in real-world applications like search engines and virtual assistants, demand robustness and precision in understanding both the question’s intent and the underlying KB structure. Current KB-QA systems often struggle with the nuances of simple questions, exhibiting limitations in accurately identifying relevant entities and relationships. The core difficulty in KB-QA stems from the complex interplay of several factors. First, converting natural language into a structured query – often a SPARQL query – requires accurate pattern extraction and entity linking. Errors introduced during these initial steps can cascade throughout the entire QA pipeline, leading to incorrect answers. This 'error propagation' problem is particularly acute in the context of simple questions, where even minor misinterpretations can significantly impact the final result. Secondly, identifying the most relevant facts within a potentially enormous KB necessitates robust fact selection mechanisms. Traditional approaches often rely on simple keyword matching or basic semantic similarity, which can be inadequate for capturing the subtle relationships expressed in natural language. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach to simple KB-QA that centers on a pattern-revising mechanism, specifically designed to mitigate error propagation and enhance fact selection. Our framework begins with standard pattern extraction and entity linking components. However, we introduce a crucial *pattern revising procedure* that dynamically adjusts the extracted patterns based on feedback from subsequent stages, actively correcting for potential errors. This iterative refinement process allows the system to adapt to the specific characteristics of each question and KB. Furthermore, to improve fact retrieval, we propose a joint fact selection strategy enhanced by relation detection. This allows us to learn a ranking function that prioritizes subject-predicate pairs likely to contain the correct answer, considering both the question and the KB context. We further strengthen our model by employing multi-level encodings and incorporating multi-dimensional information, enriching the representation of both the question and the KB entities. This holistic approach aims to capture a more comprehensive understanding of the question's meaning and its relationship to the underlying knowledge. Our experimental results, evaluated on a standard KB-QA benchmark, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance and surpassing existing methods by a substantial margin, highlighting the significant potential of pattern-revising and joint fact selection for simple KB-QA. Discourse relations, the underlying connections between segments of text, are fundamental to understanding meaning and coherence in natural language. Recognizing these relations—whether explicit or implicit—is a crucial step in many downstream NLP tasks, acting as a bridge between sentence-level understanding and higher-level text comprehension. Corresponding author, discourse relation recognition finds application in a wide range of areas, including text summarization (Yoshida et al., 2014), conversational AI (Higashinaka et al., 2014), question answering systems (Verberne et al., 2007), and even information extraction pipelines (Cimiano et al., 2005). These applications underscore the importance of robust and accurate discourse relation recognition as a core component of intelligent text processing. Generally, discourse relations are broadly categorized into two types: explicit and implicit. Explicit discourse relations are those signaled by explicit connectives—linking words or phrases that overtly indicate the relationship between segments. Implicit discourse relations, on the other hand, lack such overt markers and require a deeper understanding of the context and semantic relationships to be inferred. This distinction significantly impacts the complexity of the recognition task, with implicit relation identification posing a considerable challenge. To illustrate, consider the following example adapted from the Wall Street Journal: "The company was disappointed by the ruling. because The obligation is totally unwarranted." In this example, the connective "because" clearly signals an explicit Cause relation between the two clauses. However, many instances in natural language lack such explicit cues, necessitating more sophisticated methods to identify the underlying relationships. The reliance on explicit connectives makes explicit discourse relation recognition relatively straightforward, while the absence of such cues in implicit relations requires models to infer the relationship based on a broader range of linguistic and contextual factors. This necessitates the development of techniques capable of leveraging nuanced semantic cues and capturing intricate dependencies within the text. Traditional approaches have often relied on hand-crafted features and rule-based systems to address this challenge, but these methods can be brittle and difficult to generalize. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promise, but many models struggle to effectively capture the underlying probability distributions over discourse relations, particularly in the context of implicit relations where signal is weaker. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach based on variational inference, allowing us to model the uncertainty inherent in discourse relation recognition and learn more robust and generalizable representations. Our Variational Neural Discourse Relation Recognizer aims to tackle this challenge by incorporating the benefits of neural networks with a principled probabilistic framework. This paper investigates the application of variational autoencoders to improve discourse relation recognition, offering a more principled and potentially more accurate approach to capturing both explicit and implicit relationships within text. Our central contribution is a model that explicitly models the uncertainty in discourse relation prediction, leading to improved performance and robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on standard benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.
